title: The contour effect: Differences in the aesthetic preference and stress response to photo-realistic living environments
research_question: To investigate the contour effect (preference for curved vs. angular stimuli) in photo-realistic indoor environments, examining its impact on aesthetic preference (beauty, liking) and stress response (rest, stress), and exploring potential interactions with interior design style (modern vs. classic) and biological sex.

participants.description: 198 healthy adults (aged 18-69 years, Mdn = 27.0±10.9; 50% female participants) with no severe/uncorrected visual impairments, fluent in German, and no diagnosed mental or neurological disorder. The sample was highly educated.
participants.recruitment: Recruited via the online platform Prolific (www.prolific.co), stratified by sex (50:50).

stimuli_or_exposures.description: 20 photo-realistic images of virtual living rooms. Stimuli were exclusively manipulated on two factors: contours (angular vs. curved) and interior design style (modern vs. classic). There were 5 images for each of the four categories: angular modern (AM), curved modern (CM), angular classic (AC), and curved classic (CC). Each room included 18 objects matched in bounding sizes, materials, and colors. Images were rendered from different viewpoints (first-person perspective) within Unity.

mechanisms: Evolutionary adaptive behavior (avoidance of potentially harmful edges)
Intrinsic attractive properties of curves (good stimulus continuity)
Zeitgeist effects (time-related fluctuations in aesthetic values influenced by societal phenomena)
Biophilia hypothesis (innate evolutionary-based tendency for humans to connect with nature, curves common in nature)
Sex-related differences in neural correlates of beauty and aesthetic processing strategies
moderators: Presentation mode (static 2D images vs. immersive VR)
implementation_implications: Designs intended to promote mental-health should prioritize curved contours due to their consistent positive effects on stress responses, irrespective of style or sex.
Aesthetic preferences for contours are more complex and context-dependent, suggesting a need for nuanced design approaches based on target user groups and styles.

tables.description: Reliability of the rating scales (N=198), 5 items (5 picture per category AM, AC, CM, and CC). Cronbach's alpha and 95% confidence intervals for beauty, liking, rest, and stress across different stimulus categories.

limitations: The study was limited to explicit responses collected through self-reports, lacking the objectivity required for affirmative conclusions.
Measures lacked a common operationalization, though reliability was confirmed.
Only a small variance in aesthetic preference ratings was explained by manipulated factors (contours, style), suggesting other factors play a stronger role.
The study only tapped into a few aspects of the visual domain, which is unsurprising given the complexity of environmental influences.
The study did not assess sociological gender, making it difficult to interpret whether observed sex differences were biological or gender-related.
The online recruitment may have led to a highly educated sample, potentially affecting generalizability.
The absence of strong theoretical explanations for the psychological impact of architecture and design necessitates further exploration with more objective paradigms and different presentation modes.

paper_metadata.title: The contour effect: Differences in the aesthetic preference and stress response to photo-realistic living environments
paper_metadata.crossref_title: The contour effect: Differences in the aesthetic preference and stress response to photo-realistic living environments
paper_metadata.crossref_abstract: The interest in the response to contours has recently re-emerged, with various studies suggesting a universal preference for curved over angular stimuli. Although no consensus has yet been reached on the reasons for this preference, similar effects have been proposed in interior environments. However, the scarcely available research primarily depends on schematic or unmatched stimuli and faces heterogeneity in the reported results. In a within-subject design, we investigated the claimed contour effect in photo-realistic indoor environments using stimulus material previously tested in virtual reality (VR). A total of 198 online participants rated 20 living room images, exclusively manipulated on the contours (angular vs. curved) and style (modern vs. classic) levels. The scales represented aesthetic (beauty and liking) and stress (rest and stress) responses. Beyond our main focus on contours, we additionally examined style and sex effects to account for potential interactions. Results revealed a significant main effect of contours on both aesthetic (η2g = 1–2%) and stress (η2g = 8–12%) ratings. As expected, images of curved (vs. angular) contours scored higher on beauty, liking, and rest scales, and lower on stress. Regarding interactions with style, curvature was aesthetically preferred over angularity only within images depicting modern interiors, however, its positive effect on stress responses remained significant irrespective of style. Furthermore, we observed sex differences in aesthetic but not in stress evaluations, with curvature preference only found in participants who indicated female as their sex. In sum, our study primarily confirms positive effects of curvature, however, with multiple layers. First, the impact on aesthetic preference seems to be influenced by individual and contextual factors. Second, in terms of stress responses, which might be especially relevant for designs intended to promote mental-health, the consistent effects suggest a more generalizable, potentially biophilic characteristic of curves. To the best of our knowledge, this is the first study to demonstrate these effects in fully-matched, photo-realistic, and multi-perspective interior design stimuli. From the background of a previous VR trial from our research group, whereby the same rooms did not elicit any differences, our findings propose that static vs. immersive presentations might yield different results in the response to contours.

stimulus_description.duration_exposure: brief, image-by-image presentation (e.g., a few seconds per image)
control_conditions: angular contoured environments (as comparison for curved)

theory_commitments.specific_claim: Exposure to certain environmental features (e.g., curved contours) can reduce physiological and psychological stress.
Environments with certain characteristics (e.g., fascination, coherence) can restore directed attention and reduce mental fatigue, often linked to aesthetic preference.
Humans have an innate tendency to connect with nature and other living systems, which may explain preferences for certain natural forms like curves.

mechanism_chain.description: Curved contours are perceived as less threatening and more inviting due to evolutionary associations, leading to positive affective responses, reduced stress, and increased aesthetic preference.

instruments_used.name: Beauty ratings
instruments_used.description: Self-reported ratings on a Likert scale regarding the beauty of the presented environment.

instruments_used.name: Perceived stress ratings
instruments_used.description: Self-reported ratings on a Likert scale regarding the level of stress induced by the environment.

instruments_used.name: Heart Rate Variability (HRV)
instruments_used.description: Measures variations in the time interval between heartbeats, indicative of autonomic nervous system activity.
